teacher.title: Teacher
teacher.step.release: The object is released from rest. Initial velocity is zero at height h₀.
teacher.step.gravity_only: Only gravity acts on the object. Air resistance is ignored — ideal free fall.
teacher.step.accelerating: The object accelerates uniformly. Velocity increases linearly, displacement quadratically.
teacher.step.midpoint: Midpoint of the fall. Velocity is about 9.8 m/s. Notice the speed keeps increasing.
teacher.step.approaching_ground: Approaching the ground! Velocity nears maximum. Potential energy almost fully converted to kinetic.
teacher.step.impact: The object hits the ground. Velocity reverses direction on impact. Some energy is lost in the collision.
teacher.step.bounce: The object bounces back at 60% of impact speed. Energy is conserved but partially converted to other forms.
teacher.step.second_peak: The object reaches a new peak height, lower than the initial. It will fall again — this is real-world bouncing physics.

plugin.projectile-motion.name: Projectile Motion
teacher.projectile.step1.title: Observe Motion
teacher.projectile.step1.desc: A ball is launched at an angle. Notice its trajectory is a parabola.
teacher.projectile.step2.title: Decompose Velocity
teacher.projectile.step2.desc: Split initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components. Horizontal stays constant, vertical is affected by gravity.
teacher.projectile.step3.title: Horizontal Motion
teacher.projectile.step3.desc: No horizontal force means constant horizontal velocity.
teacher.projectile.step4.title: Vertical Motion
teacher.projectile.step4.desc: Gravity causes constant downward acceleration. At the peak, vertical velocity is zero.
teacher.projectile.step4.formula: y(t) = v0 * sin(theta) * t - 1/2 * g * t^2
teacher.projectile.step5.title: Key Parameters
teacher.projectile.step5.desc: Range, max height, and flight time are all determined by initial speed and angle. Max range at 45 degrees.
teacher.projectile.step6.title: Impact Analysis
teacher.projectile.step6.desc: The ball hits the ground. Horizontal velocity persists, vertical velocity is downward.
teacher.projectile.step7.title: Knowledge Summary
teacher.projectile.step7.desc: Projectile motion is the superposition of constant horizontal velocity and free-fall vertical motion. The two dimensions are independent.
quiz.title: Check Understanding
quiz.freefall.q1: What force acts on an object in free fall?
quiz.freefall.q1.exp: In ideal free fall (ignoring air resistance), the object is only affected by gravity.
quiz.freefall.q2: What is the relationship between velocity v and time t in free fall?
quiz.freefall.q2.exp: Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion. v = g·t, velocity is proportional to time.
plugin.inclined-plane.name: Inclined Plane
teacher.incline.step1.title: Observe Setup
teacher.incline.step1.desc: A block rests on an inclined plane. Gravity decomposes into components along and perpendicular to the incline.
teacher.incline.step2.title: Decompose Gravity
teacher.incline.step2.desc: The parallel component is mg*sin(theta). The perpendicular component is mg*cos(theta).
teacher.incline.step3.title: Force Analysis
teacher.incline.step3.desc: The incline provides normal force N = mg*cos(theta). With friction, f = mu*N, directed up the incline.
teacher.incline.step4.title: Newton 2nd Law
teacher.incline.step4.desc: Along the incline: mg*sin(theta) - mu*mg*cos(theta) = ma. If the net force is positive, the block accelerates.
teacher.incline.step5.title: Critical Angle
teacher.incline.step5.desc: When mu > tan(theta), friction is sufficient to hold the block at rest. This is called self-locking.
teacher.incline.step6.title: Reaching Bottom
teacher.incline.step6.desc: The block reaches the bottom of the incline with maximum velocity.
teacher.incline.step7.title: Knowledge Summary
teacher.incline.step7.desc: The key to incline problems is correct force decomposition. Apply Newton's 2nd law along the incline direction. Friction always opposes motion.
plugin.collision.name: Collision
teacher.collision.step1.title: Observe Motion
teacher.collision.step1.desc: Two balls approach each other. Note their masses may differ.
teacher.collision.step2.title: Momentum Calculation
teacher.collision.step2.desc: Total momentum before collision: p = m1*v1 + m2*v2. Momentum is a vector with direction.
teacher.collision.step3.title: Impact Moment
teacher.collision.step3.desc: At impact, large forces act briefly between the balls. Total momentum remains constant.
teacher.collision.step4.title: Post-collision Velocities
teacher.collision.step4.desc: Elastic collision: v1u0027 = ((m1-m2)*v1 + 2*m2*v2)/(m1+m2). If m1=m2, velocities are exchanged.
teacher.collision.step5.title: Energy Analysis
teacher.collision.step5.desc: In elastic collisions, kinetic energy is conserved. e=1 is perfectly elastic, e=0 is perfectly inelastic.
teacher.collision.step6.title: Verify Conservation
teacher.collision.step6.desc: Total momentum before and after collision are equal. Adjust parameters to verify.
teacher.collision.step7.title: Knowledge Summary
teacher.collision.step7.desc: The core of collision problems is momentum conservation. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy. The restitution coefficient describes elasticity.

plugin.spring-mass.name: Spring-Mass
teacher.spring.step1.title: Observe Setup
teacher.spring.step1.desc: A mass attached to a spring is pulled from equilibrium and released.
teacher.spring.step2.title: Hooke Law
teacher.spring.step2.desc: The spring restoring force is proportional to displacement, pointing toward equilibrium.
teacher.spring.step3.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
teacher.spring.step3.desc: Acceleration is proportional to negative displacement - the defining property of SHM.
teacher.spring.step4.title: Oscillation Period
teacher.spring.step4.desc: The period depends only on mass and spring constant, not amplitude.
teacher.spring.step5.title: Energy Conversion
teacher.spring.step5.desc: Kinetic and elastic potential energy continuously convert. Total energy is constant.
teacher.spring.step6.title: Observe Period
teacher.spring.step6.desc: Adjust mass or spring constant to see how the period changes.
teacher.spring.step7.title: Knowledge Summary
teacher.spring.step7.desc: SHM is the foundation of periodic motion. Key properties: force proportional to displacement, period independent of amplitude, energy conserved.
plugin.pendulum.name: Pendulum
teacher.pendulum.step1.title: Observe
teacher.pendulum.step1.desc: Bob released from angle, begins swinging under gravity.
teacher.pendulum.step2.title: Force Analysis
teacher.pendulum.step2.desc: Bob subject to gravity and tension. Tangential gravity drives motion.
teacher.pendulum.step3.title: Small Angle
teacher.pendulum.step3.desc: For theta < 15 deg, sin(theta) ~ theta, motion is SHM.
teacher.pendulum.step4.title: Period Formula
teacher.pendulum.step5.title: Energy
teacher.pendulum.step5.desc: Max KE at lowest point, max PE at highest. Total energy conserved.
quiz.projectile.q1: What forces act on a projectile (ignoring air resistance)?
quiz.projectile.q1.exp: After launch, only gravity acts. Horizontal velocity stays constant because no horizontal force.
quiz.projectile.q2: At the highest point of projectile motion:
quiz.projectile.q2.exp: At peak: vy=0 (vertical velocity reverses). vx stays constant. Gravity still acts (a=g).
quiz.incline.q1: On an incline, gravity mg is decomposed into:
quiz.incline.q1.exp: Gravity parallel component mg*sin(theta) drives motion along incline. Perpendicular component mg*cos(theta) is balanced by normal force.
quiz.incline.q2.exp: When mu > tan(theta), static friction is sufficient to keep the block at rest. This is the 'critical angle' condition.
quiz.collision.q1: In any collision, which quantity is ALWAYS conserved?
quiz.collision.q1.exp: Momentum is always conserved (no external forces). Kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions.
quiz.collision.q2: In a perfectly elastic collision with equal masses, what happens?
quiz.collision.q2.c: Both balls continue with same speed
quiz.collision.q2.exp: For equal masses in elastic collision: v1' = v2 and v2' = v1. The velocities swap!
quiz.spring.q1: The period of a spring-mass oscillator depends on:
quiz.spring.q1.exp: T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k). Period depends only on m and k, NOT on amplitude. This is a key property of SHM.
quiz.spring.q2: At the equilibrium position of a spring oscillator:
quiz.spring.q2.a: Velocity is maximum, force is zero
quiz.spring.q2.b: Velocity is zero, force is maximum
quiz.spring.q2.c: Both velocity and force are zero
quiz.spring.q2.exp: At equilibrium: x=0 so F=-kx=0, but velocity is maximum. All energy is kinetic (1/2 mv^2 = total E).
quiz.pendulum.q1: The period of a simple pendulum depends on:
quiz.pendulum.q1.exp: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g). Period depends only on length and gravity, NOT on mass or amplitude (small angles).
quiz.pendulum.q2: At the lowest point of a pendulum swing:
quiz.pendulum.q2.a: Speed is maximum, tension is maximum
quiz.pendulum.q2.b: Speed is zero, tension equals mg
quiz.pendulum.q2.c: Speed is maximum, tension equals mg
quiz.pendulum.q2.exp: At lowest point: max speed, max KE. Tension = mg + mv^2/L (greater than mg due to centripetal requirement).

quiz.freefall.q3: During free fall, what is the acceleration?
quiz.freefall.q3.exp: In free fall, acceleration is constant at g=9.8 m/s². This is uniformly accelerated motion.
quiz.freefall.q3.hint: Think: if we ignore air resistance, what force acts on the object? Is it constant?
quiz.freefall.q4: An object falls freely from 20m (g=10 m/s²). How long to reach the ground?
quiz.freefall.q4.exp: From h=½gt²: 20=½×10×t², t²=4, t=2s. Verify your intuition with the formula!
quiz.freefall.q4.hint: Use h=½gt², plug in h=20, g=10, solve for t
quiz.freefall.q1.hint: Near Earth's surface, what force pulls objects downward?
quiz.freefall.q2.hint: Free fall velocity formula is v=gt. The longer it falls, the faster it goes
quiz.projectile.q3: In projectile motion, how does horizontal velocity change?
quiz.projectile.q3.exp: Horizontally, there is no force, so by Newton's first law, horizontal velocity stays constant.
quiz.projectile.q3.hint: Is there any horizontal force? No force means no acceleration.
quiz.projectile.q4: An object is launched horizontally at 10 m/s. After 2s, what is the horizontal displacement?
quiz.projectile.q4.hint: Horizontal displacement = speed × time, independent of vertical motion
quiz.projectile.q1.hint: With no horizontal force, does horizontal speed change?
quiz.projectile.q2.hint: What is the initial vertical velocity?
quiz.incline.q3: On an incline, what direction is the normal force?
quiz.incline.q3.exp: Normal force is always perpendicular to the contact surface.
quiz.incline.q3.hint: Normal force = perpendicular force. Perpendicular to what?
quiz.incline.q4: On a 30° incline, the component of weight along the incline is what fraction?
quiz.incline.q4.exp: Component along incline = mg·sinθ = mg·sin30° = mg/2. Half the weight pulls it down the slope.
quiz.incline.q4.hint: Draw a force diagram: decompose weight into parallel and perpendicular components
quiz.incline.q1.hint: What direction is gravity? What force pulls it down the slope?
quiz.incline.q2.hint: Remember Newton's 2nd: F=ma. Net force determines acceleration
quiz.collision.q3: In a completely inelastic collision, what is conserved?
quiz.collision.q3.exp: Momentum is conserved in all collisions. Kinetic energy is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions.
quiz.collision.q3.hint: One quantity is always conserved in any collision. Which one?
quiz.collision.q4: A 1kg ball at 4m/s hits a stationary 1kg ball (completely inelastic). Final velocity?
quiz.collision.q4.hint: Use m₁v₁+m₂v₂=(m₁+m₂)v for completely inelastic collision
quiz.collision.q1.hint: What quantity is always conserved in collisions?
quiz.collision.q2.hint: What is special about elastic collisions?
quiz.spring.q3: What does a spring-mass system's period depend on?
quiz.spring.q3.exp: Period T=2π√(m/k) depends only on mass m and spring constant k, not amplitude.
quiz.spring.q3.hint: Recall T=2π√(m/k). Does amplitude appear in this formula?
quiz.spring.q4: A spring (k=100 N/m) is stretched 0.1m. What is the elastic potential energy?
quiz.spring.q1.hint: Who discovered that spring force is proportional to displacement?
quiz.spring.q2.hint: F=kx: greater displacement means greater force
quiz.pendulum.q3: What does a simple pendulum's period depend on?
quiz.pendulum.q3.exp: Period T=2π√(L/g) depends only on length L and gravity g, not mass or amplitude (small angles).
quiz.pendulum.q3.hint: T=2π√(L/g). Does mass appear in the formula?
quiz.pendulum.q4: A 1m pendulum has a period of approximately? (g≈10 m/s²)
quiz.pendulum.q4.exp: T=2π√(1/10)≈2π×0.316≈2s. A 1-meter pendulum swings with ~2s period.
quiz.pendulum.q1.hint: What characterizes the back-and-forth motion of a pendulum?
quiz.pendulum.q2.hint: At the highest vs lowest point, where is speed greatest?
plugin.circular-motion.name: Circular Motion
teacher.circ.step0_desc: The ball begins uniform circular motion with constant angular velocity. Centripetal force points toward the center.
teacher.circ.step1_desc: Speed is constant, but direction changes continuously. Velocity is always tangent to the circle.
teacher.circ.step2_desc: Acceleration always points toward the center. Magnitude: a = v²/r = rω².
teacher.circ.step3_desc: From Newton's 2nd Law: F = ma = mv²/r = mrω².
quiz.circ.q1: In uniform circular motion, how does speed change?
quiz.circ.q1.exp: In uniform circular motion, speed (magnitude of velocity) remains constant, but the direction changes continuously.
quiz.circ.q2: Where does the centripetal force point?
quiz.circ.q2.exp: Centripetal force always points toward the center, keeping the object in circular motion.
quiz.circ.q2.hint: The word 'centripetal' already suggests the direction.
quiz.circ.q3: When angular velocity increases, what happens to centripetal acceleration?
quiz.circ.q3.exp: Centripetal acceleration a = rω² is proportional to ω², so it increases with angular velocity.
quiz.circ.q3.hint: Look at the formula a = rω².
quiz.circ.q4: With radius 2m and angular velocity π rad/s, what is the linear speed?
quiz.circ.q4.hint: Use v = rω, with r=2, ω=π.
plugin.buoyancy.name: Buoyancy
teacher.buoy.step0_desc: The object is submerged in fluid, experiencing both gravity and buoyant force.
teacher.buoy.step1_desc: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. F_b = ρ_fluid × V × g.
teacher.buoy.step2_desc: If object density < fluid density, it floats. If greater, it sinks. If equal, it suspends.
teacher.buoy.formula2:
ρ_obj < ρ_fluid → Float
ρ_obj > ρ_fluid → Sink
ρ_obj = ρ_fluid → Suspend
teacher.buoy.step3_desc: Net force = Buoyant force - Weight = (ρ_fluid - ρ_obj) × V × g.
teacher.buoy.step4_desc: The object reaches its equilibrium position where buoyant force equals weight.
quiz.buoy.q1: What does the buoyant force equal?
quiz.buoy.q1.exp: Archimedes Principle: An object submerged in fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
quiz.buoy.q1.hint: Remember Archimedes' discovery in the bathtub.
quiz.buoy.q2: What condition causes an object to sink in a fluid?
quiz.buoy.q2.exp: When ρ_obj > ρ_fluid, gravity exceeds buoyant force and the object sinks.
quiz.buoy.q2.hint: Compare the object density with fluid density.
quiz.buoy.q3: A steel block sinks in water, but a steel ship floats. Why?
quiz.buoy.q3.c: Water has more friction on the ship
quiz.buoy.q3.exp: The ship's hollow shape increases its displaced volume, greatly increasing buoyant force. F_b = ρ_fluid × V_displaced × g.
quiz.buoy.q3.hint: Think about the shape and displacement of ships.
quiz.buoy.q4: When an object is suspended in a fluid, what is the relationship between densities?
quiz.buoy.q4.exp: At suspension, buoyant force = weight: ρ_fluid×V×g = ρ_obj×V×g, so ρ_obj = ρ_fluid.
quiz.buoy.q4.hint: Suspension means the object can rest at any depth.

teacher.coulomb.step1_desc: Two charged spheres at a distance. Electrostatic repulsion exists between them.
teacher.coulomb.step2_desc: F = k·q₁·q₂ / r². Force is inversely proportional to distance squared.
teacher.coulomb.step3_desc: Under electrostatic repulsion, the movable charge moves away. As distance increases, force decreases.
teacher.coulomb.step4_desc: Coulomb force is an inverse-square law, similar to gravity. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
teacher.refraction.step1_desc: Light travels from medium 1 (n₁) toward the boundary with medium 2 (n₂).
teacher.refraction.step2_desc: Snell Law: n₁·sinθ₁ = n₂·sinθ₂. The refraction angle depends on the refractive indices.
teacher.refraction.step3_desc: In medium 2, the light direction changes. If n₂ > n₁, light bends toward normal; if n₂ < n₁, light bends away.
teacher.refraction.step4_desc: Refraction occurs because light travels at different speeds in different media. Refractive index n = c/v.
teacher.doppler.step1_desc: Sound source moves at constant speed. As it approaches the observer, wavelengths are compressed.
teacher.doppler.step2_desc: Doppler formula: f = f·v_sound / (v_sound ∓ v_source). Frequency rises when approaching, falls when receding.
teacher.doppler.step3_desc: After passing the observer, frequency drops sharply. This is why ambulance sirens change pitch.
teacher.doppler.step4_desc: Doppler effect is used in radar speed guns, medical ultrasound, and astronomical redshift measurements.

plugin.ac_generator.name: AC Generator
teacher.generator.step1_desc: Water, steam or a hand crank drives the coil to rotate uniformly in the magnetic field. Mechanical energy enters the system.
teacher.generator.step2_desc: The flux through the coil, Phi = BA·cos(wt), varies periodically as the coil rotates. This is the source of the induced EMF.
teacher.generator.step3_desc: EMF = NBAw·sin(wt): both magnitude AND direction vary sinusoidally — this is alternating current. Watch the current arrows flip every half turn.
teacher.generator.formula2: EMF = N B A w sin(wt)
teacher.generator.step4_desc: A generator uses two complete slip rings to output AC; a motor uses a split commutator to keep torque one-directional. This is the key structural difference.
